title: Delhi High Court Case Tests Whether India Can Deny OCI Cards Without Giving a Reason
excerpt: The Wire founder Siddharth Varadarajan's fight to convert his expired PIO card to OCI status has become a precedent-setting battle over government accountability and the rights of overseas Indians.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Delhi High Court quashed government's rejection of Varadarajan's OCI application for lack of reasons.
  • The court later recalled its order after discovering Varadarajan's non-disclosure of bail conditions.
  • The case has broader implications for millions of former PIO cardholders facing conversion deadlines.
  • Physical PIO cards are invalid for travel to India since January 1, 2026, necessitating OCI conversion.
  • The Delhi High Court initially quashed the government's rejection of journalist Siddharth Varadarajan's PIO-to-OCI conversion, ruling the refusal contained no reasons and "cannot be sustained."
  • The court later recalled its own order after the government revealed Varadarajan had not disclosed bail conditions from an Allahabad High Court order restricting his travel.
  • The case is now listed for further hearing, with the court demanding Varadarajan explain the non-disclosure via affidavit.
  • The ruling has broader implications for the estimated millions of former PIO cardholders whose physical cards expired on December 31, 2025.

A Routine Conversion Becomes a Legal Battle

When India merged its Person of Indian Origin card scheme into the Overseas Citizen of India program, the government set a December 31, 2025 deadline for PIO cards to remain valid for travel. For most of the roughly 4 million PIO cardholders worldwide, the transition was administrative. For Siddharth Varadarajan, the founding editor of The Wire and a US citizen who has lived in India since 1995, it became a legal confrontation with the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Varadarajan applied to convert his PIO status to OCI after his physical card became unreadable and therefore invalid for entry into India. On April 2, 2026, the MHA rejected his application — without providing any reasons for the denial.

MHA rejects Varadarajan's OCI application without providing reasons.
May 12, 2026

May 14, 2026
Government reveals Varadarajan's non-disclosure of bail conditions, court recalls its order.
Upcoming Hearing
Court to determine implications of non-disclosure on Varadarajan's case.

Court Rules Rejection Was Unreasoned

Varadarajan challenged the rejection in the Delhi High Court. On May 12, Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav sided with him, finding that the government's communication contained no reasons and could not be sustained.

"Unless the respondent assigns the reasons, the appellate court may not be able to appreciate the matter. The reasons are the heart and soul of the order," Justice Kaurav said, setting aside the rejection and directing the government to reconsider the application and issue a reasoned decision.

Senior Advocate Nitya Ramakrishnan, appearing for Varadarajan, argued that PIO cardholders were automatically deemed OCIs under law after 2015, and that her client merely needed a physical card that matched his existing legal status.

Suppression Allegation Reverses Course

Two days later, the case took a sharp turn. The government, represented by Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, informed the court that Varadarajan had failed to disclose a 2020 Allahabad High Court order imposing conditions on his bail in a separate case — including a requirement that he not leave India without the trial court's permission and that he surrender his passport.

Justice Kaurav recalled his earlier order, saying Varadarajan appeared "prima facie guilty of suppressing material facts." He directed the journalist to file an affidavit explaining why the bail conditions were not disclosed, warning of "serious consequences."

Varadarajan's counsel apologized, saying the non-disclosure was unintentional and had "skipped her mind." The court was not satisfied: "We have to test your forgetting of this order. If we accept apology like this then it will lead to a serious situation in court."

"Reasons are the heart and soul of the order. The impugned communication is set aside."

— Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav, Delhi High Court

What It Means for PIO and OCI Holders

The case has been listed for further hearing, with the Centre given time to file a counter-affidavit. While the specific facts involve a high-profile journalist with a pending criminal case, the underlying legal question — whether the government can reject PIO-to-OCI conversions without explanation — has implications for overseas Indians broadly.

Since January 1, 2026, physical PIO cards are no longer valid for travel to India, making conversion to OCI essential for anyone who held the older document. The court's initial ruling that an unreasoned rejection cannot stand would, if upheld, require the government to provide substantive grounds for any denial — a standard that could protect ordinary applicants who lack the resources to challenge bureaucratic decisions in court.

The next hearing is expected to determine whether Varadarajan's non-disclosure of bail conditions disqualifies him from relief entirely, or whether the government must still justify its original rejection on independent grounds. The case is being closely watched by immigration lawyers and diaspora organizations tracking India's evolving approach to its overseas citizens.

Impact on PIO Cardholders
›4 million PIO cardholders affected by conversion deadline.
›Physical PIO cards expired on December 31, 2025.
›Court ruling may require government to justify OCI application rejections.
›Significant implications for ordinary applicants lacking legal resources.
